cases.title: Recurrent variceal bleeding and TIPS
cases.stem: A 56-year-old man with cirrhosis has recurrent variceal bleeding despite optimal pharmacological and endoscopic therapy. TIPS is being considered.

questions.question: What is the principal haemodynamic aim of a TIPS?
options: Create a portosystemic shunt that reduces the portal pressure gradient
questions.explanation: TIPS creates a low-resistance communication between the portal and systemic venous circulations to decompress portal hypertension.

questions.question: Which pre-procedural assessment is particularly important when estimating the risk of post-TIPS decompensation?
options: Cardiac function and evidence of right-sided heart failure
questions.explanation: TIPS increases venous return and may precipitate cardiac decompensation; cardiopulmonary assessment is therefore important.
questions.newInfo: There is no active infection and renal function is preserved.

questions.question: During creation of the TIPS tract, which structures are usually connected?
options: A hepatic vein and a portal vein branch
The hepatic artery and portal vein
The inferior vena cava and renal artery
The splenic vein and inferior mesenteric vein
questions.explanation: The intraparenchymal tract connects a hepatic vein with a portal vein branch.
questions.imageFile: Fluoroscopic image of transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) in progress.jpg

questions.question: The patient develops severe refractory hepatic encephalopathy after TIPS. Which interventional option may be considered?
questions.explanation: TIPS reduction can decrease excessive portosystemic shunting in selected patients with refractory encephalopathy.

cases.title: Pelvic trauma embolisation
cases.stem: A haemodynamically unstable patient has an unstable pelvic fracture and arterial contrast extravasation on CT despite ongoing resuscitation.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly supports urgent angiography and embolisation?
options: Active arterial extravasation with persistent transfusion requirement
An isolated pelvic fracture in a stable patient
Pelvic pain without evidence of bleeding
questions.explanation: Active arterial bleeding with haemodynamic compromise is a classic indication for urgent endovascular haemostasis.

questions.question: A focal bleeding branch of the internal iliac artery is identified. What is the main advantage of selective embolisation when feasible?
options: It treats the culprit vessel while limiting non-target ischaemia
It requires embolisation of the entire abdominal aorta
It avoids the need for angiographic confirmation
It guarantees that rebleeding cannot occur
questions.explanation: Selective treatment aims to control the culprit branch while preserving as much uninvolved pelvic circulation as possible.

questions.question: Which embolic agents may be appropriate depending on anatomy and bleeding pattern? Choose all that apply.
options: Liquid embolic agents in selected situations
Room air as a standard embolic agent
questions.explanation: Coils, gelatin and selected liquid agents may all be appropriate; room air is not a standard therapeutic embolic agent.

questions.question: Place the following steps in a reasonable procedural order.
options: Selective catheterisation of the suspected vessel
questions.explanation: A logical sequence is arterial access, diagnostic angiography, selective catheterisation, then embolisation and completion angiography.

questions.question: For renovascular hypertension caused by renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia, the usual first-line endovascular treatment is:
questions.explanation: Balloon angioplasty is usually preferred; stenting is reserved for selected complications or inadequate results.

questions.question: Which finding supports clinically relevant May-Thurner syndrome?
options: Left common iliac vein compression with ipsilateral thrombosis and venous collaterals
An isolated right popliteal artery aneurysm
questions.explanation: Anatomical compression becomes clinically meaningful when accompanied by venous obstruction, thrombosis or collateralisation.

questions.question: In life-threatening haemoptysis, the bleeding source most commonly arises from:
options: The pulmonary artery in every case
questions.explanation: Most severe haemoptysis treated by embolisation originates from hypertrophied bronchial or non-bronchial systemic arteries.

questions.question: The primary objective of uterine artery embolisation for fibroids is to:
options: Occlude the proximal internal iliac arteries permanently
Reduce perfusion of the fibroid bed while avoiding non-target embolisation
questions.explanation: UAE targets the uterine/fibroid arterial supply while preserving non-target pelvic territories.

questions.question: Catheter-directed therapy for acute iliofemoral DVT is most appropriately considered in:
options: All patients with isolated distal DVT
Selected patients with extensive symptomatic iliofemoral DVT and low bleeding risk
Patients with chronic bilateral ankle oedema and no thrombosis
questions.explanation: Endovascular thrombus removal is reserved for selected patients; it does not routinely replace anticoagulation.

questions.question: Which complication should be specifically considered after percutaneous thermal ablation of a renal tumour?
options: Haemorrhage and thermal injury to adjacent structures
questions.explanation: Bleeding and injury to bowel, ureter or other adjacent structures are important procedure-related risks.

questions.question: In an infected obstructed collecting system, the immediate purpose of percutaneous nephrostomy is to:
options: Perform definitive stone fragmentation in every case
questions.explanation: Urgent drainage controls obstruction and infection; definitive treatment of the cause usually follows after stabilisation.

questions.question: Which measure reduces occupational radiation exposure during fluoroscopic intervention?
options: Stand close to the X-ray tube whenever possible
Use collimation, shielding and distance appropriately
Remove protective shielding to improve access
questions.explanation: Time, distance, shielding and collimation are fundamental principles of radiation protection.
